title: Scale a Poisson mean to a longer interval
source: S2 Ch2 theory S2-2.2 Quick check 1 (5 every 10 minutes, so 15 in 30 minutes)
stem: Events occur at a mean rate of {r|int} every {t|int} minutes. What is the Poisson parameter for a {T|int}-minute interval?

steps.name: form
steps.text_tex: The new interval is \({k|int}\) times as long, so the mean is scaled by \({k|int}\).
steps.note: The mean is proportional to the length of the interval.

contexts.stem: Calls arrive at a mean rate of {r|int} every {t|int} minutes. What is the Poisson parameter for a period of {T|int} minutes?
Faults occur at a mean rate of {r|int} every {t|int} metres. What is the Poisson parameter for a length of {T|int} metres?

title: Scale a Poisson mean when the rate is not an integer
source: S2 Ch2 theory S2-2.2 Quick check 2 (1.2 every 4 minutes, so 3 in 10 minutes)
stem: Calls arrive at a mean rate of {R|dp1} every {t|int} minutes. What is the Poisson parameter for a {T|int}-minute interval?

steps.name: form
steps.text_tex: The mean scales in the ratio of the intervals, \(\dfrac{{T|int}}{{t|int}}\).
steps.note: The mean is proportional to the interval.

contexts.stem: Events occur at a mean rate of {R|dp1} every {t|int} minutes. Find the Poisson parameter for an interval of {T|int} minutes.
If the mean number of arrivals in {t|int} minutes is {R|dp1}, what is the mean number in {T|int} minutes?

title: Scale a per-hour rate down to a shorter interval
source: S2 Ch2 theory S2-2.2 Quick check 3 (3 per hour, so 1 in 20 minutes)
stem: A machine produces faults at a mean rate of {h|int} per hour. What is the Poisson parameter for a {m|int}-minute interval?

steps.name: form
steps.text_tex: \({m|int}\) minutes is \(\dfrac{{m|int}}{60}\) of an hour, so the mean is scaled by that fraction.
steps.note: Convert to a fraction of an hour.

contexts.stem: Events occur at a mean rate of {h|int} per hour. Find the Poisson parameter for {m|int} minutes.
If the mean number of events per hour is {h|int}, what is the mean number in {m|int} minutes?

title: 9709/72/M/J/16 Q6(i): demand in a two-week period

source.note: Stem verbatim from the QP PDF, part (i) only, including the official wording 'per week' and 'two-week period'. Later parts of Q6 (stock levels for one week) are omitted. Fully manual, because the official answer is a Poisson probability. Official MS: lambda=6.8 (B1), Poisson P(X=5) (M1), 0.135 to 3 s.f. (A1). Independently exp(-6.8) times 6.8^5 / 120 = 0.13495..., which is 0.135 to 3 s.f.

stem:
At a certain shop the demand for hair dryers has a Poisson distribution with mean 3.4 per week.

(i) Find the probability that, in a randomly chosen two-week period, the demand is for exactly 5 hair dryers.

steps.name: lam
steps.text_tex: A two-week period has Poisson parameter \(\lambda=2\times 3.4=6.8\).

steps.name: form
steps.note: Official MS: Poisson P(X=5) with any λ.

steps.name: E
steps.text_tex: The probability is \(0.135\) to 3 significant figures.

title: 9709/71/O/N/14 Q6(i): accidents in an 18-week period

source.note: Stem verbatim from the QP PDF, part (i) only, including the official wording 'per 12-week period' and '18-week period'. Parts (ii)–(iv) (Type I and Type II errors after a new junction) are omitted because they belong to hypothesis testing in a later subsection. Fully manual. Official MS: lambda=4.65 (B1), Poisson P(X=4) (M1), 0.186 to 3 s.f. (A1). Independently lambda=3.1*18/12=4.65 and exp(-4.65) times 4.65^4 / 24 = 0.18626..., which is 0.186 to 3 s.f.

stem:
The number of accidents on a certain road has a Poisson distribution with mean 3.1 per 12-week period.

(i) Find the probability that there will be exactly 4 accidents during an 18-week period.

steps.name: lam
steps.text_tex: The mean scales in the ratio of the intervals: \(\lambda=3.1\times\dfrac{18}{12}=4.65\).

steps.name: form
steps.note: Official MS: Poisson P(X=4) with any λ.

steps.name: E
steps.text_tex: The probability is \(0.186\) to 3 significant figures.
